item.title: 2 days before the election, poll shows voters overwhelmingly want change
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
NBC News Democrats have a sizable advantage in the battle for control of Congress days ahead of the midterm elections, a new national NBC News poll finds, with voters clamoring for change and voicing all-time high disapproval of President Donald Trump. Registered voters prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress by a 7-point margin, with Democrats leading Republicans 52%-45% — 2 points more than in last month ’s poll. That includes a 21-point lead among independents. Three percent of voters remained undecided as the poll was conducted from Oct. 28 to Oct. 30, and how they shift in the final days could tilt the outcome in dead-heat House and Senate races around the country. While the overall poll suggests that Democrats are poised to capitalize on a well of dissatisfaction with the president and his policies, there are findings that complicate the favorable picture. When it comes to which party better handles key issues, voters give Republicans and Democrats about even marks, and the Democratic Party remains deeply unpopular. Meanwhile, Republican voters in GOP-held districts and in states Trump won in 2024 are sticking with their party — which is notable because much of the battle for control of both the House and Senate runs through this red terrain. But there are also numerous signs of trouble for the GOP, with Trump at the center of a difficult political environment for Republicans and their slim majorities in both houses of Congress. The president’s disapproval rating has climbed to 60%, a new high mark in the NBC News poll across his two terms, and his approval rating stands at 40%. After Trump won a second term in 2024 promising to bring down prices and restore the economic conditions of his first term, roughly 3 in 4 voters head into the midterms dissatisfied with the state of the economy. Nearly two-thirds of voters are calling for a change from the direction Trump has been leading the country, with 50% calling for “a great deal” of change, a new high mark in NBC News polling data. And for the first time in 30 years of NBC News polling, more voters say they are dissatisfied with their financial situation (51%) than satisfied (49%). “The Trump presidency can be summarized as the promise of two years ago and the peril of two days from now,” said Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the survey with Republican pollster Bill McInturff of Public Opinion Strategies. Horwitt noted Trump returned to the White House after promising economic prosperity and peace. But now voters are expressing widespread concerns about the economy, with prices rising during the Iran war. Amid those concerns, 64% of voters — including a third of Trump voters — say the president has fallen short of their expectations, with 34% saying he has lived up to them. Seventy percent of voters say the country is on the wrong track, a 9-point increase over the last year. Voters continue to rank inflation and the cost of living as the most important issues facing the country, followed by government corruption, threats to democracy and immigration and border security. “Democrats are in total control of the 2026 issue agenda,” said McInturff, the Republican pollster, noting that only voters who think immigration is a top issue are breaking for his party right now. Democrats have a 1-point advantage on which party would better control inflation, a slight decline from September but still a warning sign for the GOP, which led on the issue in 2024. Republicans have a 2-point advantage on the economy, a marked decline from the party’s double-digit advantage on the issue in recent years. Voters are also signaling that they are fired up about the midterms, with 70% ranking themselves as a “9” or “10” on a 10-point scale of interest in the election. Democrats have a 12-point advantage among those most-engaged voters, while Republicans have a 2-point edge among voters who are less interested in the election. Self-described MAGA Republicans also say they’re significantly more interested in the election than Republicans who don’t identify with the MAGA wing, as Trump and his party push to turn out voters who typically sit out midterm elections. That dynamic could be one reason why Republicans have leaned into culture war arguments in key races, attacking Democrats on transgender issues. The new poll shows a potential limitation of that strategy: Democrats have a 5-point advantage on the question of which party would better handle transgender issues, despite those Republican attacks. It’s not all good news for Democrats, and the poll contains fresh signs that a number of voters are pushing back on the GOP, as opposed to falling in love with the Democratic Party, which remains deeply unpopular. Just 29% of voters view the Democratic Party positively, while 38% have positive views of the Republican Party. Around half of voters have negative views of both parties. Still, some voters who are wary of Democrats are still planning to support them this year. “Republicans have proven that they are not to be trusted. So I would rather see the balance of power shift, than maintain one party’s control,” one poll respondent from Texas, who voted for Trump in 2024 and is supporting Democrats for Congress this year, said in an expanded response. “I don’t trust Republicans or Democrats, really,” the man added. Republican disappointment Frustrations among voters like that man from Texas, who backed Trump in 2024 and typically backs Republicans, are dragging down the president and GOP candidates this year. Republicans are torn on whether the country is moving in the right direction (48%), or the wrong direction (43%). One year ago, Republicans said the country was going in the right direction, 75%-24%. Now, a majority of Republicans (53%) are dissatisfied with the state of the economy. And 37% of Trump’s own party believe he’s fallen short of his promises. Trump still maintains an important hold on his base, with near-unanimous job approval (93%) among Republicans who say they support the MAGA movement. But he’s slipped significantly with Republicans who don’t consider themselves part of the MAGA movement: 54% of them approve and 46% disapprove of his performance. Meanwhile, 20% of those non-MAGA Republicans say they prefer to see Democrats control Congress after this election. The president has seen other important voting blocs drift away, too. His net approval rating has dropped 18 points among white voters without college degrees compared to the first NBC News poll of his second term , in 2025. He’s also seen significant declines among young voters and Latino voters, groups that he overperformed with on his way back to the White House in 2024. One of Republicans’ big advantages in 2026 is a favorable political map: Democrats have to win back districts and states Trump won in 2024 to take back Congress. In the Senate, they need to win at least two states Trump carried by double-digit margins. But the president’s approval rating is underwater in states he won in 2024: 53% of registered voters there disapprove of his job performance, while 47% approve. In March 2025, his approval rating in those states was 10 points higher. Democratic warning signs There are some warning signs for Democrats, on top of the fact that a lower share of voters have positive views of the Democratic Party compared to the Republican Party. The fight for control of the House and especially the Senate will take place in Trump-won areas, and Republicans are leading on the congressional ballot in GOP-held districts and in states Trump won in 2024. The big question is whether that’s enough to withstand shifts in some key places. Government corruption has been a central theme of Democrats’ message this year, but voters narrowly trust Republicans to better handle the issue by 5 points. Even so, Democrats are leading on the congressional ballot among the 28% of voters who do not trust either party on the issue. Republican leaders in Congress are also slightly better off than their Democratic counterparts, but that’s mostly because voters don’t know how to feel about them. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., has the highest positive rating of congressional leaders: 24% have positive views of him and 34% have negative views. Just 10% of voters have positive views of Johnson’s counterpart across the Capitol, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, while 22% view him negatively. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries is viewed positively by 18% of voters and negatively by 35%. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who’s led Democrats in the body for almost a decade, is far better defined — to his detriment. Just 13% of voters view him positively, and 53% view him negatively. “It’s not great for the Democrats … for 2028,” said McInturff, the Republican pollster, when asked about the low marks for Democrats. “But I don’t see it as a barrier for how well they can do in 2026 when midterms are about Trump and these economic numbers.” Half of voters have negative views of tech billionaire Elon Musk, who has emerged as one of the most prolific Republican donors in the country over the last two years, while 34% view him positively. Voters are more split about a pair of prominent progressives, Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Sanders is more popular: 41% view him positively and 42% view him negatively, while Ocasio-Cortez’s numbers stand at 31%-42%. Democrats hold a significant lead in the battle for Congress despite those factors. But there are indications throughout the poll that the party’s lead is propped up strongly by anti-Republican sentiment, not warm feelings for Democrats. Voters who want Democratic control of Congress are divided between whether their vote is more in favor of Democrats or driven more by opposition to Republicans. “Get your s--- together, Democrats,” an Ohio Democratic woman said when asked what message she wanted to send with her vote this year. “I’m voting for you, but work it out.” The NBC News poll surveyed 1,000 registered voters Oct. 28-30 via a mix of telephone interviews and an online survey sent via text message. The margin of error is plus or minus 3.1 percentage points. item.title: Trump to deliver final midterm pitch at problem-plagued Lincoln Memorial pool
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump is making his closing pitch of the midterm elections at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool , pushing his slow, expensive and problem-plagued efforts to repair it back into the spotlight on the eve of Election Day . In comments to reporters as he deplaned from Air Force One for a Sunday rally in Iowa, Trump said his speaking at the site would “show how beautiful it is.” “We might hold it tomorrow or something,” the president added, without giving specifics. Hours later, the White House formally announced he'd be giving a speech there Monday afternoon. Rather than using Monday to travel to key states and try to energize his “Make America Great Again” supporters as his Republican Party tries to maintain control of Congress, Trump opted for an event at a Washington renovation project that has been embarrassing and contentious. The unusual move marks a departure from Trump's month-long race to stage more than 25 rallies in largely conservative areas, hoping the GOP can overcome his own low approval ratings and polls predicting that the Iran war , high energy prices and cost of living increases could spell a strong election night for Democrats . Trump wrote on his social media site that his Sunday evening rally in Kansas — which followed his Iowa visit — was “my last stop.” The presidewnt spent a lot of time at those rallies talking about his second-term focus on molding the White House and the surrounding nation's capital in his own image. He crammed the Oval Office with gold flourishes , demolishing the East Wing to construct a sprawling ballroom , converting the Rose Garden into a patio space reminiscent of his Mar-a-Lago estate and erecting a sprawling South Lawn helipad. Trump also closed the Kennedy Center after failed attempts to add his name to the building , has planned a towering arch just outside the city and is pushing to revamp a century-old public golf course . He has bristled at criticisms from former President Barack Obama and other Democrats that he's spent too much time focused on construction projects — insisting that renovations relax him and that he does them quickly and without requiring too much planning time. Trump said the Reflecting Pool fix would be fast and inexpensive His Reflecting Pool saga began in April when Trump said he wanted to change its color and would use contractors he knew to fix the monument in mere days and for about $1.5 million before Independence Day. The repairs wrapped up nearly three months behind schedule and the budget ballooned to more than 10 times Trump's early estimate — and that's assuming no more additional work will need to be done in the future. Trump had initially declared the work was complete in June. But after unveiling the overhaul, the pool was soon choked with algae blooms , and its “American-flag blue” liner began peeling off in sections. The pool was quickly drained anew for repairs in mid-July. Trump has repeatedly blamed vandals, but the office of U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia — former Fox News host and longtime Trump ally Jeanine Pirro — said the problems were caused by shoddy workmanship . In his comments Sunday, Trump continued to insist that the Reflecting Pool “was vandalized badly.” He said that security cameras have since been added to stop that. Still, a particularly ignominious moment came when the Justice Department charged former Olympian David Hearn with intentionally damaging the Reflecting Pool — then abruptly dropped the case this summer — determining he was not responsible. A judge later permanently dismissed it. That prompted Trump to fume that Pirro “choked,” and that he was "disappointed with Jeanine Pirro, really disappointed. She folded like an umbrella” — though he stopped short of firing her. item.title: 4 Americans among dozens killed in last week's train crash in Spain, officials say
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Four United States citizens were among the at least 69 people who were killed when a high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train in central Spain last week, officials said Sunday. The Center for Integrated Data, the legal body in Spain in charge of identifying victims of events with a high death toll, said on Sunday night that the casualties in the country's second deadly rail collision this year also included one citizen each from Canada, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Tunisia and the Czech Republic. Two citizens of Australia and a citizen of Japan remain missing, the Agence France-Presse and local media reported. The center, which had already announced the deaths of a French and Portuguese citizen as well as 54 Spaniards, said that all but three of the victims had been identified. "As the contacted families have expressed their wish to travel to Spain to carry out in-person identification, we are awaiting their arrival in the country," the statement said, AFP reported. The crash occurred on the morning of Oct. 28 in Urda, in the province of Toledo, when the high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars. Officials said 58 people were injured. The two trains, with more than 540 people on board, were heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville. Transport Minister Óscar Puente has blamed a traffic controller's poor judgment for much of what went wrong. However, railway unions have pushed back, citing deteriorating working conditions. They say too few controllers are handling growing workloads, making it increasingly difficult to ensure the safety of millions of passengers. The independent investigators said their initial findings indicated that the state-owned RENFE train was moving at between 100 and 125 mph when it struck the privately owned IRYO train. It was the second major crash on the Madrid-Seville line this year. In January , more than two hours farther south along the route, a train derailed and struck another traveling in the opposite direction, killing 46 people. That crash remains under investigation. Spain's high-speed rail network, the world's second-largest after China's, has long been regarded as a success of state industrial policy. Until this year, it had recorded no fatal crashes since entering service more than three decades ago. item.title: AI stocks just lost $5 trillion — but the stock market's sweetest stretch might be now
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The AI trade just had its scariest October in years. The rest of the stock market barely noticed. The biggest AI and chip stocks have shed about $5 trillion in market value since Oct. 6, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Nvidia ( NVDA ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ) have each given up roughly $835 billion in market cap, and Intel ( INTC ) lost nearly half its value in October. Everything else? The other 625 large US stocks in that tally added about $1.3 trillion. And while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) slipped this week, 9 of its 11 sectors rose about 1% or more, something that hadn’t happened in any week since at least 1999, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Yahoo Finance Jeff Hirsch, editor of the Stock Trader's Almanac , has a name for this: "Octoberphobia." And he's buying the sell-off. "I did buy some today... this is an opportunity here," Hirsch told Yahoo Finance on Friday . "The damage isn't as bad as the headlines are." Hirsch also has the calendar on his side. October selloffs like this one often lead into what the Almanac calls the sweet spot of the presidential election cycle , which runs from the fourth quarter of a midterm year through the following June. History is on the buyers' side From the last October close of a midterm year to the end of the following June, the S&P 500 has risen 19 times out of 19 since 1950 , with a median gain of about 15%. Chip stocks have been 8-for-8 since 1994, with a median gain of about 22%. Yahoo Finance The ride wasn't always smooth. Chips fell another 11% or so before turning higher in 2002 and 2018, and eight cycles is a relatively small sample. Chips just sprang a possible bear trap The iShares Semiconductor ETF ( SOXX ) tumbled about 17% in October, yet it's still up more than 50% this year. On Friday, it dipped as low as $460, below the $464 low from July 29 that marked this summer's bottom. Then it closed at $472, back above that line. That's the look of a bear trap — a breakdown that reverses, catching traders betting on more losses. Chip stocks briefly broke below their July low Friday, then closed back above it. Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace Hirsch likes the timing. "Historically, seasonally, it sets up great for this period of time, the best months of the year for semiconductors," he said. His firm placed a new buy in the sector on Friday. Bulls first need to reclaim about $524, the top of last week's bounce, then the early-October high near $596. Losing the July low would put the February-April range near $370 in play. That's about 21% below Friday's close. The case for waiting Not everyone is loading up the shopping cart. BofA's Michael Hartnett said it's "risk-off until global rate hike ends," pointing to 42 central bank rate hikes worldwide over the past six months. The Fed held on Wednesday , but two officials voted to hike. Hartnett's line in the sand for chips is $520 on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF ( SMH ), which closed Friday near $522. On SOXX, that works out to about $469, just above the July low it barely held. So the bulls' and bears' lines sit almost on top of each other. Hirsch said he'd change his view on a decisive break of the S&P 500's mid-September low near 7,550, less than 1% below Friday's close. Tuesday's midterm vote comes first. Then November, the S&P 500's best month of the year , gets its turn. Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. Humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked this post before publication. Jared Blikre is the global markets and data editor for Yahoo Finance. Follow him on X at @SPYJared or email him at jaredblikre@yahooinc.com. item.title: At 11th hour, Dem Haley Stevens endorses Republican Mike Rogers in Mich. Senate race
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
DETROIT (AP) — Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary , Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers as Democratic tensions boiled over days before the election that could determine the balance of power on Capitol Hill. Stevens endorsed Rogers after attending a Detroit church service with him. The remarkable show of support for the President Donald Trump-backed candidate in the tightly contested race comes after she was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed, who defeated the congresswoman by a slim margin in the August primary. “Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away," Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement, which led her top aide to quit. “And he's right. And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.” El-Sayed dismissed the endorsement when asked about it by reporters later Sunday, saying he's focused on issues voters care about, such as the high cost of living. “At the end of the day I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens," he said, adding later: “None of this matters." Michigan Democratic leaders were left shocked. With just less than 48 hours to go before Election Day, a party that had spent months trying to unite behind its Senate nominee was suddenly grappling with an extraordinary defection in one of this year's most important races. Tensions between the two Democrats have festered since the primary. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the U.S. ally. He has also been criticized by some in the community for past remarks regarding a Michigan synagogue attack and for appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker . El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, is facing Rogers, an ex-congressman, for the seat held by the retiring Democrat, Gary Peters. Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party’s effort to win a majority for the final two years of Trump’s second term. Stevens and El-Sayed were originally scheduled to attend church together, along with other Michigan and national Democrats, including South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn. Democrats hoped it would be a show of unity as they worked to boost turnout in the Detroit area, where concerns have lingered about enthusiasm among Black and Jewish voters in key Democratic strongholds. Instead, Stevens swayed to gospel music alongside Rogers in the pews at Perfecting Church, while El-Sayed was a few miles away at a different house of worship campaigning alongside prominent Democrats, including Clyburn. In an at times disjointed interview later Sunday night on CNN, Stevens said she decided to back Rogers after waking up in the morning and having time to think. “This is a weight off my shoulders, I’m being straight with everybody,” Stevens said, describing El-Sayed as increasingly angry. She at times took long pauses and seemed to struggle to explain her decision. U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan, who joined CNN's Anderson Cooper immediately after his interview with Stevens, said it was “one of the most painful interviews I have watched” and that she has been worried all week about Stevens. Stevens' team resigns as Democrats are stunned by reversal After the church service north of Detroit, where Stevens and her fiance Jason Turkish worshipped with Rogers and his wife, Kristi, the congresswoman told reporters, “I’m not turning my back on Democrats. It is this one vote.” Rogers, standing beside her, said he was “honored” by her support. Their appearance came days after Stevens publicly reaffirmed she would vote for her party's nominee. It also led her longtime chief of staff to resign, with a number of staff members expected to follow soon, according to a person familiar with the developments who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters. “We are shocked and heartbroken,” the aide said in a statement. The state party chair, Curtis Hertel, said Stevens' endorsement “shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about.” “We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum," Hertel wrote, and won't let such 11th-hour “distractions” deter the campaign. Hertel later wrote that Stevens "is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future." Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, who supported Stevens in the primary, denounced her endorsement of Rogers. “This is a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens,” Schumer wrote in a social media post. Dingell says she disinvited Stevens after it became ‘distracting’ Among the Democrats who joined El-Sayed at church Sunday morning were Dingell, U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the Senate primary before voting began. Dingell, a senior Democratic figure in the state who helped organize the planned joint appearance, said she asked Stevens not to attend and that Stevens told her she would abide by that. “I'm the one who pulled it, because it had become way too distracting," Dingell said in an interview before Stevens appeared with Rogers. “This is not how I was going to spend my weekend before the election, to be perfectly frank.” In the August primary, Stevens defeated El-Sayed in Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and neighboring Oakland County, drawing support from Black and Jewish voters who are important parts of the Democratic coalition. Early voting for Tuesday's election has been underway since Oct. 24. As of Friday, more than 1.8 million people had already voted in Michigan. How did we get here? The Democratic primary was among the most bitter this year. Each candidate accused the other of making personal attacks. Tens of millions of dollars in outside spending poured into the race, including from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s affiliated super PAC, which backed Stevens. El-Sayed took particular offense to an outside group’s ad accusing him of disrespecting women. Although Stevens pledged after the primary to help El-Sayed however she could, the two have not appeared together publicly since a unity breakfast two days after his primary win. Last week Stevens’ fiance told The Detroit News that he would vote for Rogers. Stevens later appeared on CNN to reaffirm her support for El-Sayed but urged his campaign to “shut out the hate and call it out.” But on Friday, after The Associated Press reported on the planned joint appearance, Stevens released a lengthy statement calling on El-Sayed to condemn an ad by an independent left-wing group that linked U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices. “Abdul promises to get money out of politics,” Stevens wrote. “He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.” El-Sayed responded: “So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand.” He made clear the ad was not made by his campaign and said “I do not agree with the contents of that ad.” Trump and Republicans revel in the discord Trump praised Stevens in a Truth Social post, saying she was “a Highly Respected Democrat” and that her support from Black and Jewish voters in Michigan is “virtually unprecedented.” “Haley said what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did,” Trump wrote. “It’s a thing called bravery, and few people have it like just displayed by Congresswoman Haley Stevens!” Appearing with Trump in Iowa for a campaign rally, House Speaker Mike Johnson said that he spoke to Stevens after she endorsed Rogers. Johnson said he “encouraged her to stay safe and keep speaking the truth.” A spokesman for the Republican National Committee, Hunter Lovell, said Democrats who feel abandoned by El-Sayed “have a home” with Rogers. ___ Cappelletti reported from Washington. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/michigan-democrats-unity-push-falters-160726549.html

item.title: All 9 people on board plane killed after it crashes in Florida, federal officials say
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A Learjet that Gov. Ron DeSantis said looked "like a missile going down" crashed Sunday near Greenacres killing all nine aboard and leaving a large swath of the area in fire and scattered debris. The plane, according to federal authorities, had departed Austin, Texas and was headed to the Bahamas. The plane crashed into a mobile home neighborhood around 12:50 p.m. in the area of Military Trail and 10th Avenue North, causing debris across a large area, but, according to DeSantis, no reported injuries or deaths from people on the ground. DeSantis was at the crash site Sunday evening and described it as a "cataclysmic plane crash." More: 'We're gonna crash! ... 'We're out of time' among last words from pilot More: Thunderstorms were firing on Sunday near where a Lear jet went down More: Learjet jet crash that killed nine was 'cataclysmic,' DeSantis says The governor said federal aviation officials were expected in Palm Beach County as soon as Sunday night and would conduct their investigation into the cause. All nine people aboard the plane died, said Sean Duffy, the U.S. secretary of transportation, in a post on X, formerly Twitter, just before 4 p.m. He called the crash a "horrific tragedy." The FAA said the Learjet 60 departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport and was headed to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas. “We’re out of time,” the pilot can be heard saying in air traffic control audio circulated online shortly before the Learjet crashed near Greenacres. The FAA and National Transportation Safety Board will investigate. The NTSB will be in charge of the investigation and will provide all updates. The incident closed all lanes of Military Trail in the area of Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North, the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said. Postings on Facebook show a fairly wide swath of area spotted with fires, debris and what looks like a crater in the ground. A video circulating online of a plane making a nosedive into the ground is said to be the Learjet, but The Palm Beach Post is not sharing that video as it has not been confirmed. The video is said to be from a driver's dashcam video. The cause of the crash is unknown. Some chatter on social media raised the suspicion that the plane could have been shot down because flight restrictions were in place as President Donald Trump was in town this weekend . Trump departed President Donald J. Trump International Airport for Iowa around noon. Planes that fly into the restricted airspace are diverted, usually by military jets. Multiple planes have violated the airspace since Trump first took office, but a plane has never been shot down in Palm Beach County because of the airspace violations. The upgraded security systems, a pair of Avenger Air Defense Systems , are positioned on a floating barge in the Lake Worth Lagoon on the west side of Trump's Mar-a-Lago. A separate bank of Avenger Air Defense Systems are positioned on the south side of Trump international airport, near the area where Air Force One parks during Trump's visits to Palm Beach. The Avenger's targets could include cruise missiles, drones, helicopters and low-flying and high-speed fixed-wing aircraft, according to the Army. As of Sunday night, there was no indication the Learjet was shot down. Weather conditions in the West Palm Beach area on Sunday afternoon were rough with thunderstorms widespread because a stalled frontal boundary parked over the area, pushing freezing cloud tops tens of thousands of feet high — a situation that can cause icing trouble with equipment but also from severe turbulence. The crash site is in an unincorporated area near Greenacres and Palm Springs. The Village of Palm Springs said it has officials on the scene monitoring any effect the crash will have on water and sewer services. item.title: Democratic Senator Chris Murphy hospitalized after stroke, chief of staff says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy has been hospitalized after suffering a stroke, his chief of staff said in a statement on Sunday. The 53-year-old Democrat was taken to a hospital on Saturday after he started to feel numbness in his arm while attending his son's hockey game, said Allison Herwitt, Murphy's chief of staff. ABC News - PHOTO: Sen. Chris Murphy, pictured here in this appearance on ABC's "This Week," Feb. 9, 2025, was hospitalized, Oct. 31, 2026, after suffering a stroke, a top aide to the Connecticut Democrat said. Upon examining Murphy, doctors determined he had suffered a stroke, Herwitt said, adding that the senator has been transferred to Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore. "The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery," Herwitt said. No further information was released about Murphy's condition. For the past several weeks, Murphy has been traveling the country campaigning for Democratic candidates in Tuesday's midterm elections. He was scheduled to appear Sunday with Democratic Senate candidate Chris Pappas in New Hampshire, according to the New Hampshire Democratic Party. Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says In 2024, Murphy won his third term to serve Connecticut in the U.S. Senate and has been viewed by some Democratic party officials as a possible candidate for president in 2028. Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont released a statement on social media on Sunday saying he and his wife, Annie, are keeping Murphy and is family "in our prayers." "Just two days ago, I was with Senator Chris Murphy doing what he loves most: Encouraging Connecticut residents to make their voices heard and vote on Tuesday," Lamont said. "There is no stronger advocate for our democracy. And no one who fights harder for the people of this state. Chris is a great friend to Connecticut and to me personally." "I am sure that he will be walking across the state again very soon. And we will all be cheering him on," Lamont added. This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.
